newsitem.title: USA: Florida judge curbs punitive claims on tobacco companies.
newsitem.headline: Florida judge curbs punitive claims on tobacco companies.

text.p: A state judge on Tuesday cut back the billions of dollars Florida can seek in its anti-tobacco lawsuit and ruled state lawyers must prove tobacco companies were capable of making safer cigarettes.

In a flurry of decisions ahead of a trial scheduled to begin Aug. 4, Palm Beach County Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen said the 1994 Florida law that is the state government's main vehicle for suing tobacco companies did not allow for punitive damages.

Florida claims it spent $1 billion since 1994 treating sick smokers through its Medicaid healthcare program and expects to spend another $17 billion on smokers with lung cancer and other diseases in coming years.
"The legislature said, 'You can only get back the money expended'. And, if there is fraud or criminal activity, you can go after it under (other) laws as they exist," Cohen said in court.

But Cohen let stand unprecedented claims for triple damages on alleged racketeering by the tobacco companies. Those claims, alleging the tobacco companies conspired to hide the dangers of smoking, rely on Florida's anti-rackeetering law.
In addition, Cohen said Florida could pursue limited additional damages if it can prove fraud by tobacco companies through advertising or false claims made after 1982.

Cohen, who is pressing ahead with trial preparations despite last week's $368.5 billion deal on tobacco lawsuits, also ruled that Florida must prove in a trial that tobacco companies could have made safer cigarettes and hid the dangers of smoking from Americans.

An attorney for Philip Morris, one of the tobacco companies fighting the Florida suit, said Cohen's rulings mean Florida must also prove that cigarette makers in some way made tobacco use more dangerous than it otherwise would have been. Tobacco companies have fought repeated efforts to force disclosure of additives and other ingredients in cigarettes. Anti-tobacco critics claim the additives may make smoking riskier.
After the ruling, an attorney pressing the state's lawsuit, Robert Montgomery, said, "This merely narrows the issues. It shows us where we need to zero in to prove what is wrong with the product."

Earlier Tuesday, Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth denied a published report that Florida was among several states negotiating with tobacco companies about delaying a start of its Medicaid lawsuit.

The report, in The Wall Street Journal, said Texas and Florida were bargaining over trial delays with an eye to securing concessions from cigarette companies and to allow Congress time to pass laws locking in place the terms of last week's deal.

The suits of Mississippi, Texas and Florida are scheduled for trial this summer. Like 37 others filed by state governments, their suits seek damages on behalf of taxpayers for billions of dollars spent treating sick smokers through government healthcare programs.
